clue.text: This Booker winner's entry seemed to find us tolerant

definitions.text: This Booker winner's entry seemed to find us tolerant

parts.words: This Booker winner's entry seemed to find us tolerant
parts.note: the Booker-winning book's title sounds as though it calls its readers patient, that is, tolerant

explanation.surface: A prize-winning novel's title seems to compliment its readers on their forbearance.
explanation.walkthrough: The 1992 Booker winner was The English Patient; 'patient' is the 'tolerant' the clue plays on, so the entry is its author.
explanation.definitionFit: He wrote The English Patient, joint winner of the 1992 Booker Prize.

clue.text: Julia had absolute protection

parts.note: in Sheridan's The Rivals, Julia is the ward of Sir Anthony Absolute, so she is under Absolute's protection

explanation.surface: A woman named Julia enjoyed complete security.
explanation.walkthrough: 'absolute' looks like a plain adjective, but it is the surname of Sir Anthony Absolute in Sheridan's comedy The Rivals, whose ward Julia is.
explanation.definitionFit: Julia's surname in Sheridan's comedy The Rivals is Melville.

clue.text: Shaw's officer aimed a little too high, it seems

parts.note: a captain is a commissioned officer
to shoot over is to aim above the target

explanation.surface: A soldier in a Shaw play seems to have missed by firing high.
explanation.walkthrough: Captain Shotover is the old sea captain in Shaw's Heartbreak House; 'it seems' admits that his name reads as a description of bad marksmanship.
explanation.definitionFit: The old sea captain of Heartbreak House is one of Shaw's best-known characters.

clue.text: His Reminiscences include Adelina Patti and one well-known kiss

definitions.text: His Reminiscences include Adelina Patti and one well-known kiss

parts.words: His Reminiscences include Adelina Patti and one well-known kiss
parts.note: the conductor-composer wrote memoirs, worked with the soprano Patti, and wrote the waltz song Il Bacio, The Kiss

explanation.surface: A memoir recalls a famous soprano and a celebrated kiss.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'kiss' is the song Il Bacio by Luigi Arditi, who conducted for Adelina Patti and published My Reminiscences.
explanation.definitionFit: Luigi Arditi, Italian conductor, wrote My Reminiscences and the song Il Bacio.

clue.text: Existentialist entomology with an Electra complex?

definitions.text: Existentialist entomology with an Electra complex?

parts.words: Existentialist entomology with an Electra complex?
parts.note: a play by the existentialist Sartre titled after insects and retelling the Electra and Orestes story

explanation.surface: A Freudian joke about a philosopher studying insects.
explanation.walkthrough: Sartre's play The Flies retells the Electra myth; 'entomology' points to its insect title and 'Electra complex' to its story, not to Freud.
explanation.definitionFit: Sartre's 1943 play The Flies reworks the tale of Electra and Orestes.

clue.text: Powell narrator recalled in prison?

definitions.meaning: Jenkins is the narrator of Anthony Powell's A Dance to the Music of Time
slang for a jail or police station

explanation.surface: A novelist's storyteller remembers being locked up.
explanation.walkthrough: Powell's narrator Nick Jenkins recalls the whole Dance to the Music of Time; 'nick' is also British slang for prison.
explanation.definitionFit: Nick Jenkins narrates Powell's novel sequence, and a nick is British slang for a jail.

clue.text: First man on dam in Stevenson book

indicators.note: in a down clue, one piece placed on another sits above it

parts.note: Adam was the first man in Genesis
a weir is a low dam across a river

explanation.surface: Adam stands on a dam in a story by Stevenson.
explanation.walkthrough: Adam Weir, Lord Hermiston, is the hanging judge of Stevenson's unfinished Weir of Hermiston.
explanation.definitionFit: The judge Lord Hermiston, a character of Stevenson's last novel, is named Adam Weir.

clue.text: Not these revised journals of Carol Shields

indicators.note: something revised has been reworked, so these words are rearranged

parts.note: diaries are daily journals

explanation.surface: These are not the edited journals of the novelist Carol Shields.
explanation.walkthrough: 'revised' turns NOT THESE into THE STONE.
explanation.definitionFit: The Stone Diaries is Carol Shields's Pulitzer-winning novel.

clue.text: Ruth McKinney's sister

parts.note: the writer Ruth McKenney wrote stories about her sister, collected as My Sister ...

explanation.surface: A question about a writer's sibling.
explanation.walkthrough: Ruth McKenney's book My Sister Eileen became a play and the musical Wonderful Town.
explanation.definitionFit: Ruth McKenney's sibling is the title figure of her book My Sister Eileen.

clue.text: "This is a slight unmeritable man, Meet to be sent on errands." (Julius Caesar)

definitions.text: "This is a slight unmeritable man, Meet to be sent on errands." (Julius Caesar)

parts.words: "This is a slight unmeritable man, Meet to be sent on errands." (Julius Caesar)
parts.note: Antony's dismissive words about his fellow triumvir in Julius Caesar, Act 4

explanation.surface: A quotation from Shakespeare's Julius Caesar about a lightweight man.
explanation.walkthrough: Antony speaks these lines about the third triumvir once he has left the stage.
explanation.definitionFit: Antony says this of Lepidus, the third triumvir, in Julius Caesar.

clue.text: Australian begetter of reportedly noble house

definitions.text: Australian begetter of reportedly noble house

parts.words: Australian begetter of reportedly noble house
parts.note: the Sydney-born novelist who wrote Noble House, a novel about a Hong Kong trading company

explanation.surface: An Australian founded an aristocratic dynasty, so it is said.
explanation.walkthrough: 'noble house' looks like an aristocratic family, but it is the title of James Clavell's novel Noble House; Clavell was born in Sydney.
explanation.definitionFit: James Clavell, born in Australia, wrote the novel Noble House.

clue.text: How performing arts communicate, say, is paradoxically static

definitions.meaning: performing arts reach audiences by being acted out, live

explanation.surface: Performance art conveys meaning in a way that is oddly motionless.
explanation.walkthrough: Split as two words it means acted out; as one word it means idleness, hence 'paradoxically'.
explanation.definitionFit: Performing arts work by being acted out, while a lack of activity is a static state.

clue.text: Bandage in Akondate he reveals

annotationWithheld.why: Clue as held is 'Bandage in Akondate he reveals': it must be hidden in 'Akond of Swat he', after Lear's poem The Akond of Swat, but the OCR mangles more than three letters and there is no scan

clue.text: He supported a motion at Oxford

definitions.text: He supported a motion at Oxford

parts.words: He supported a motion at Oxford
parts.note: not a debating motion but the Oxford Movement, whose supporters wrote the Tracts for the Times

explanation.surface: An Oxford Union debater backed a proposal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'motion' suggests a debating motion, but the Oxford Movement is meant, named after its Tracts for the Times.
explanation.definitionFit: An adherent of the Oxford Movement, after its Tracts for the Times.

clue.text: Leaders of Lanark and Nithsdale gentry reveal Scottish writer

indicators.note: the leaders of the following words are their opening letters

explanation.surface: Lanarkshire and Dumfriesshire gentry unveil a Scottish author.
explanation.walkthrough: Andrew Lang, born in Selkirk, wrote the coloured Fairy Books.
explanation.definitionFit: Andrew Lang was a Scots poet and folklorist famous for his Fairy Books.

clue.text: "I will chastise you with -" (Rehoboam)

parts.note: King Rehoboam in 1 Kings 12 says his father chastised with whips, he will use stinging creatures

explanation.surface: A biblical king's threat, with its last word missing.
explanation.walkthrough: Rehoboam answers the people: 'my father chastised you with whips, but I will chastise you with scorpions'.
explanation.definitionFit: Rehoboam's threat in 1 Kings 12 ends with these stinging arachnids.

clue.text: "Quick — darting through the brain" (Pope)

parts.note: a line from Pope's Essay on Man about scents that could overpower us, with the key word missing

explanation.surface: A line of Pope's verse with a word left out.
explanation.walkthrough: Pope's Essay on Man: 'Or quick effluvia darting through the brain, / Die of a rose in aromatic pain'.
explanation.definitionFit: Pope's line in An Essay on Man speaks of quick effluvia, emanations of scent.

clue.text: Trojan opener adds a run, tentatively

indicators.note: something done tentatively is tried one way and another, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A cricket opening batsman tentatively scores a run.
explanation.walkthrough: 'opener' suggests a cricket batsman; here it is the founder of the Trojan royal line. 'tentatively' rearranges ADDSARUN.
explanation.definitionFit: Dardanus founded the line of Trojan kings, so he opens Troy's story.

clue.text: C.S. Forester proposed death to them

definitions.text: C.S. Forester proposed death to them

parts.words: C.S. Forester proposed death to them
parts.note: Forester's Napoleonic-war novel bears a title calling for death to Britain's old enemy across the Channel

explanation.surface: A novelist called for the killing of some people.
explanation.walkthrough: C. S. Forester's Hornblower-era novel is Death to the French.
explanation.definitionFit: Forester's novel Death to the French gives the people wished dead.

clue.text: That of death saves a man, said Forster

definitions.text: That of death saves a man, said Forster

parts.words: That of death saves a man, said Forster
parts.note: Forster wrote in Howards End that death destroys a man but the notion of death saves him

explanation.surface: A novelist claims that something about death can rescue a man.
explanation.walkthrough: From Howards End: 'Death destroys a man: the idea of Death saves him.'
explanation.definitionFit: Forster's line says the idea of Death saves a man.

clue.text: His wife refused to turn over a page

definitions.text: His wife refused to turn over a page

parts.words: His wife refused to turn over a page
parts.note: in A Midsummer Night's Dream the fairy queen will not hand her changeling page boy to her husband

explanation.surface: A wife would not turn the page of a book.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turn over a page' suggests reading; it means hand over a page boy, the changeling Titania refuses to give her husband.
explanation.definitionFit: The fairy king in A Midsummer Night's Dream quarrels with Titania over her changeling page.

clue.text: … moreover including, we hear, Wellsian islander and Flaubert hero

indicators.note: we hear means the letters are taken from how the word is said, not how it is spelt

parts.note: the word moreover begins with the sound more-oh

explanation.surface: Two characters, one from Wells and one from Flaubert, are added together.
explanation.walkthrough: 'including' says the name sits inside 'moreover' by sound: the first two syllables, more-oh. Dr Moreau rules H. G. Wells's island; Frédéric Moreau is the hero of Sentimental Education.
explanation.definitionFit: Dr Moreau is Wells's island vivisector and Frédéric Moreau Flaubert's hero in Sentimental Education.

clue.text: Olivia Manning's was lost and won

definitions.text: Olivia Manning's was lost and won

parts.words: Olivia Manning's was lost and won
parts.note: the title of a novel in Manning's Levant Trilogy describes a fight that was lost and won

explanation.surface: Olivia Manning both lost and won something.
explanation.walkthrough: The first of Manning's Levant Trilogy is The Danger Tree; the second is The Battle Lost and Won.
explanation.definitionFit: Manning's novel The Battle Lost and Won names the fight.

clue.text: Operetta buff from Chamonix?

definitions.meaning: a devotee of Gilbert and Sullivan, named after the Savoy Theatre
Chamonix lies in the French Alpine region of Savoy, so a native belongs to it

explanation.surface: A light-opera enthusiast who hails from an Alpine resort.
explanation.walkthrough: Gilbert and Sullivan operas were staged at London's Savoy Theatre; Chamonix is in Savoie.
explanation.definitionFit: Gilbert and Sullivan fans take their name from the Savoy Theatre, and Savoie's natives share it.

clue.text: Smart fellow? (His rival was an Angel)

definitions.meaning: in Hardy's Tess of the d'Urbervilles, Tess is wooed by Angel Clare and his rival d'Urberville

explanation.surface: A clever man had a heavenly competitor.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Angel' is Angel Clare, not a heavenly being; his rival for Tess is Alec d'Urberville.
explanation.definitionFit: A smart alec is a know-all, and Alec d'Urberville rivals Angel Clare for Tess.

clue.text: "The history of art is the history of s" (Samuel Butler)

definitions.text: "The history of art is the history of s" (Samuel Butler)

parts.words: "The history of art is the history of s" (Samuel Butler)
parts.note: Butler's Notebooks say art's history is a series of returns to earlier styles; the word's plural ending is printed

explanation.surface: A Butler epigram about art history with its key word missing.
explanation.walkthrough: Butler's Note-Books: 'The history of art is the history of revivals.' The printed 's' is the plural ending, leaving the singular.
explanation.definitionFit: Butler's line says the history of art is the history of revivals.

clue.text: Describing sojourns by Brenan, Campbell and Lee (for, ie, brain regeneration?)

definitions.text: Describing sojourns by Brenan, Campbell and Lee

indicators.note: regeneration means the letters are made anew in a different order

explanation.surface: A note on travel writers in Spain, with a joke about brains.
explanation.walkthrough: Gerald Brenan, Roy Campbell and Laurie Lee all lived in Spain; 'regeneration' rearranges IEBRAIN.
explanation.definitionFit: All three writers lived in Spain, on the peninsula shared with Portugal.

clue.text: Squat men Connors recast in Ayckbourn piece

indicators.note: to recast is to rework or cast anew, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Squatting men named Connors are recast in an Ayckbourn play.
explanation.walkthrough: 'recast' rearranges SQUATMENCONNORS.
explanation.definitionFit: Alan Ayckbourn's trilogy The Norman Conquests is one of his best-known works.
